'''Egusi sauce''' or egusi soup a popular soup in Nigeria<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Giwa |first1=Solomon O. |last2=Akanbi |first2=Taiwo O. |title=A Review on Food Uses and the Prospect of Egusi Melon for Biodiesel Production |journal=BioEnergy Research |volume=13 |issue=4 |pages=1031–1045 |year=2020 |doi=10.1007/s12155-020-10145-4}}</ref><ref>{{cite journal |last1=Datsugwai |first1=Mohammed Sani Sambo |last2=Aisha |first2=Abdulkadir |last3=Balogu |first3=Tochukwu Vincent |title=Microbial Quality and Sensory Characteristics of Instant Nigerian Egusi Soups |journal=Annals: Food Science and Technology |volume=20 |issue=3 |pages=494–501 |year=2019}}</ref>. The word 'Egusi' is of Yoruba origin<ref>{{Cite web |title=Egusi Soup – Lumpy Yoruba Style – 9jafoodie {{!}} Nigerian Food Recipes |url=https://9jafoodie.com/yoruba-style-egusi-soup/ |access-date=2026-05-09 |language=en-US}}</ref><ref>{{cite journal |last1=Ilori |first1=T. A. |last2=Akinyele |first2=O. A. |last3=Aremu |first3=D. O. |title=Effect of Moisture Content on Some Engineering Properties of Celosia argentea Seed |journal=Journal of Environmental Science, Toxicology and Food Technology |volume=10 |issue=9 |pages=157–160 |year=2016}}</ref>. It is prepared with [[Egusi|egusi seeds]] as a primary ingredient.<ref>{{cite book
 | last = Bowen
 | first = T. J.
 | title = Central Africa: Adventures and Missionary Labors in Several Countries in the Interior of Africa, from 1849 to 1856

}}</ref><ref name="TWC">{{cite book | url=https://books.google.com/books?id=GmqEAwAAQBAJ&pg=PA239 | title=The World Cookbook: The Greatest Recipes from Around the Globe, Revised Edition | pages=239–240| isbn=9781610694698 | last1=Jacob | first1=Jeanne | last2=Ashkenazi | first2=Michael | date=2014-01-15 | publisher=Abc-Clio }}</ref> Egusi seeds are the [[fat]]- and [[protein]]-rich [[seed]]s of certain [[cucurbitaceous]]  (squash, melon, gourd) plants. Egusi sauce is common and prevalent across [[Central Africa]] as mbíka, and may be served atop rice, cooked vegetables, or grilled meat, such as goat, chicken, beef, or fish.<ref name="TWC" /><ref name="WP" /><ref name="Katende" /> It may also be served atop [[fufu]], omelettes, [[Amala (food)|amala]], and [[eba]],<ref name="WP">{{cite news | url=https://www.washingtonpost.com/pb/recipes/goat-and-beef-with-egusi-sauce/12614/ | title=Goat and Beef With Egusi Sauce | newspaper=[[The Washington Post]] | date=February 29, 2012 | accessdate=5 September 2014}}</ref><ref>{{cite book | url=https://books.google.com/books?id=n6m-yHGupq0C&pg=PA19 | title=Veg Out Vegetarian Guide to Washington,, Part 3 | pages=19| isbn=9781586854713 | last1=Evans | first1=Andrew | year=2004 | publisher=Gibbs Smith }}</ref><ref>{{cite book | url=https://books.google.com/books?id=nmorHDWeih4C&q=%22Egusi+sauce%22 | title=Around the world in 450 recipes | accessdate=5 September 2014 | pages=26| isbn=9781844775279 | last1=Ainley | first1=Sarah | year=2008 | publisher=Hermes House }}</ref><ref>{{cite book | url=https://books.google.com/books?id=id1lAAAAMAAJ&q=%22Egusi+sauce%22 | title=Roots in the Sky | pages=211| isbn=9789780645403 | last1=Adesokan | first1=Akinwumi | year=2004 | publisher=FESTACBooks }}</ref> among other foods. <!-- Eba is a [[staple food]] eaten in [[West Africa]], particularly in the Southern and Western parts of [[Nigeria]] made from [[cassava]] (manioc) flour. --> Egusi soup is also consumed in West Africa, sometimes with chicken.<ref>{{cite book | url=https://books.google.com/books?id=FJxlWwrVcKcC&pg=PA54 | title=The Recipes of Africa | page=54}}</ref>
